items.anchor: Introduction
items.note: Must read, 10 min. The chapter in one line: take the deterministic kinematics, add noise to the motion parameters, and you have p(xₜ ∣ uₜ, xₜ₋₁) in two forms, a density to evaluate and a sampler to run forward.

items.anchor: Motion models comprise the state transition probability
items.note: WHY: this is the predict half of every filter in ch. 3 and 4. The EKF needs it linearized (ch. 7), the particle filter needs it sampled (Table 4.3 line 4), the grid filter needs it evaluated (Table 4.1 line 3). CODE: C2–C4.

items.anchor: No model of manipulator kinematics will be provided
items.note: PITFALL: planar kinematics only, no dynamics. ROBOT: the drone is a dynamics problem (book exercises 1–3 are the first step); the quadruped is excluded explicitly on p. 121.

items.anchor: successful in practical applications vastly overestimate the amount
items.note: WHY: inflated motion noise is the cheap insurance against unmodelled state (track slip, a carpet edge) and against filter approximations. ROBOT: the ch. 4 T5 showed the same thing from the other side: at the true noise the particle filter was overconfident.
Skim 5.2.1 (5 min), must read 5.2.2 (10 min). Pose conventions, then the one distinction that matters: velocity commands for planning, odometry for estimation.

items.anchor: The conﬁguration of a rigid mobile robot is commonly
items.note: DEFINE: 6-DoF configuration (x, y, z, roll, pitch, yaw); the book drops to 3-DoF pose. ROBOT: the drone and the quadruped's body need all six; that is SE(3), lesson t2.6.
SHAPES: pose (x, y, θ) ∈ ℝ² × S¹. θ is an angle: every difference of two θ's goes through wrap() before it is used (models.py).

items.anchor: we postulate that a robot with orientation θ = 0 points
items.note: DEFINE: θ = 0 along +x, counterclockwise positive, the same convention as ROS REP 103 for the base frame (from outside the book).
Must read, 10 min. One density, (5.3), and two ways to feed it.
WHY: the object of the whole chapter. SHAPES: xₜ, xₜ₋₁ ∈ ℝ³ poses; uₜ is (v, ω) in 5.3 and a pair of odometry poses in 5.4. CODE: C3 and C4 evaluate it, C2 and C4 sample it.

items.anchor: The darker a location,
items.note: FIGURE: the density is 3-D; the plot drops θ. A crescent in x-y is the shadow of a curved 3-D cloud in (x, y, θ), a sheet exactly when α₅ = α₆ = 0. Lecture Fig L3a colours the samples by θ′ to show the sheet.

items.anchor: for conceptual reasons we will refer to ut as control
items.note: WHY: odometry is a measurement used as if it were a control (p. 133). The price: its noise enters the motion model, not the measurement update, and successive odometry errors are assumed independent.

items.anchor: The ﬁrst assumes that the motion data ut speciﬁes the
items.note: DEFINE: velocity model = what the robot was told to do; odometry model = what the wheels report it did.

items.anchor: odometry models are usually applied for estimation, whereas
items.note: WHY: odometry exists only after the motion, so a planner cannot use it. ROBOT: on the tracked robot skid-steer slip degrades track odometry in turns; whether the book's claim (pp. 121, 132) that odometry beats the commands survives that is untested on your hull. T5's simulation says it does once spins are modelled; check it on your logs.

items.anchor: The velocity motion model assumes that we can control
items.note: Must read for 5.3.1–5.3.2 and the first half of 5.3.3 (75 min); skim the inverse derivation (pp. 129–132) but derive (5.17)–(5.25) once by hand.

items.anchor: such as robots equipped with Mecanum wheels or legged robots
items.note: PITFALL: 'without non-holonomic constraints' means holonomic: they can move sideways. ROBOT: the quadruped's body twist (vₓ, v_y, ω) does not fit (v, ω); book exercise 7 generalizes the model.
SHAPES: u = (v, ω) in m/s and rad/s; positive ω turns left. CODE: C2, C3.

items.anchor: We arbitrarily postulate that positive rotational velocities ωt induce a
items.note: DEFINE: right-handed, z up. A sign flip here mirrors every trajectory; test with a left turn first.
Must read, 25 min. Table 5.1 is an inverse model: from two poses it recovers the (v̂, ω̂, γ̂) that would explain them, then scores the gap to the commanded (v, ω, 0).

items.anchor: assuming that the control is carried out for the ﬁxed duration
items.note: WHY: Δt is part of the model. The same (v, ω) over 0.1 s and over 1 s give different shapes; α's tuned at one rate do not transfer.

items.anchor: under a zero-centered random variable with variance
items.note: DEFINE: prob(a, b²) takes the variance, not the standard deviation. Every b² in this chapter is a variance. CODE: C1.

items.anchor: The velocity motion model, for different noise parameter settings.
items.note: FIGURE: same (v, ω), three α settings. (a) moderate; (b) small angular, large translational error: spread along the arc; (c) large angular error: spread across it. SESSION: the session redraws this with sliders on α₁–α₆.
Must read, 20 min. Table 5.3 is (5.16) with noise drawn on (v, ω) and a final rotation γ̂.

items.anchor: Sampling from a conditional density is different than calculating
items.note: WHY: the particle filter needs only the sampler; grid filters and scan matchers need the density. Most bugs live in the density, because it inverts the kinematics.

items.anchor: Table 5.1
items.note: Implement. CODE: C3 motion_model_velocity. PITFALL: line 7 v̂ = Δθ r*/Δt carries the sign of Δθ, not of the motion: run in this repo, (v, ω) = (1, −0.5) from (0, 0, 0), Δt = 1, gives v̂ = −1; reversing (−1, 0.5) gives v̂ = +1. The card fixes the sign and a test covers right turns and reversing. Line 2 divides by zero for straight motion; line 6 and line 9 need wrap().

items.anchor: Algorithms for computing densities of a zero-centered normal
items.note: Implement. CODE: C1 prob_normal, prob_triangular. Both take the variance b². PITFALL: b² = 0 when v = ω = 0 (robot at rest) gives 0/0; floor b².

items.anchor: Table 5.3
items.note: Implement. CODE: C2 sample_motion_model_velocity. PITFALL: lines 5–6 divide by ω̂; at ω̂ = 0 use the straight-line limit x′ = x + v̂Δt cos θ. Line 7: wrap θ′.

items.anchor: Note that we are perturbing the ﬁnal orientation
items.note: WHY: without γ̂ every sample lies on a 2-D sheet in 3-D pose space (p. 129); γ̂ thickens it. α₅, α₆ set its size.

items.anchor: Algorithm for sampling from (approximate) normal and triangular
items.note: Implement. CODE: C1 sample_normal (the sum of 12 uniforms), sample_triangular. In practice use rng.normal; the 12-uniform version is what you write on a microcontroller without a Gaussian generator. EXERCISE: book exercise 8 proves the variances; planned for T2.

items.anchor: Sampling from the velocity motion model, using the same parameters as
items.note: FIGURE: 500 samples from Table 5.3 with the α's of Fig 5.3. Compare panel by panel: the samples are the density's shape, plus sampling variance (ch. 4, Fig 4.6).

items.anchor: We note that in many cases, it is easier to sample xt than calculate the
items.note: WHY: the forward model needs only kinematics; the density needs the inverse, which for the velocity model is the circle construction of pp. 130–131. ROBOT: a learned or simulator-based motion model can only be sampled.
Must read pp. 125–129 (exact motion, real motion, final orientation, 30 min); skim pp. 129–132 but derive (5.17)–(5.25) by hand.

items.anchor: Figure 5.5
items.note: FIGURE: constant (v, ω) for Δt moves the robot on a circle of radius |v/ω| about (x_c, y_c), at 90° to the heading. Note the |·| in (5.5): the radius is unsigned, the centre side comes from the sign of v/ω in (5.7)–(5.8).
DEFINE: r = |v/ω|. ω = 0 is a straight line (r = ∞), which every formula with v/ω has to special-case.

items.anchor: Equation (5.5) encompasses the case where the robot does not turn at all
items.note: PITFALL: the book treats ω = 0 as a limit; code divides by it. CODE: C2 uses a threshold |ω| < 1e-9 and the straight-line formula, as the ch. 3 package's models.py already does.
Derive. Centre x_c = x − (v/ω) sin θ. With (5.8), the centre sits at distance v/ω to the left of the heading (right for negative v/ω).
Derive. y_c = y + (v/ω) cos θ. TEST: check the centre is equidistant from start and end pose.
Implement and derive. CODE: C2 velocity_kinematics, the noise-free g(u, x) of the ch. 3 EKF. TEST: as ω → 0 it converges to the straight line; compare at ω = 1e-6.

items.anchor: it is therefore common practice to use small values for
items.note: WHY: the circle assumes (v, ω) constant over Δt. ROBOT: at a high control rate the arc is nearly a line and the velocity and odometry models agree (p. 136).

Implement. Noise on the controls, not on the pose: the posterior is curved (a banana), which is why the EKF needs the control-noise Jacobian in ch. 7. SHAPES: two scalars, variances α₁v² + α₂ω² and α₃v² + α₄ω².

items.anchor: the standard deviation of the error is proportional to the
items.note: WHY: σ = √(α₁v² + α₂ω²) scales with the speed: double (v, ω), double σ. A robot at rest has zero motion noise, so add a floor if your filter must survive being pushed.

items.anchor: Probability density functions with variance b2
items.note: FIGURE: two zero-mean densities with the same variance b²; the triangle has bounded support (−√6 b, √6 b).
Implement. CODE: C1 prob_normal = Table 5.2 line 2. In practice use the log density and sum, as in ch. 4.
Implement. CODE: C1 prob_triangular. PITFALL: bounded support means zero probability for any error beyond √6 b; one outlier odometry step kills every particle or grid cell. Use it only with a floor.
Derive. (5.9) with (v̂, ω̂). Still degenerate: the end pose lies on a 2-D sheet. The next page fixes it.

items.anchor: However, this model is still not very realistic
items.note: WHY: two noise variables cannot fill a 3-D pose space. Read on to (5.14).

items.anchor: The assumption of circular motion leads to an important degeneracy
items.note: WHY: given (x′, y′) the circle fixes θ′ exactly, so p(xₜ ∣ uₜ, xₜ₋₁) is zero almost everywhere in (x, y, θ). A grid or a scan matcher evaluating it would see zero for nearly every cell.
Implement. θ′ = θ + ω̂Δt + γ̂Δt. CODE: C2 line 7 of Table 5.3.
Implement. γ̂ has variance α₅v² + α₆ω². DEFINE: a final rotation rate, multiplied by Δt in (5.14).
Implement. The full generative velocity model: Table 5.3 lines 5–7. CODE: C2.

items.anchor: the motion probability would simply be zero without
items.note: WHY: the density needs γ̂ for the same reason the sampler does: almost no (xₜ₋₁, xₜ) pair lies on a circle that also matches θ′.
Derive by hand: the centre lies on the line through (x, y) perpendicular to the heading, and on the perpendicular bisector of the chord. Two lines, one intersection.

items.anchor: case of ω = 0, in which the center of the circle lies at
items.note: PITFALL: (5.18)'s denominator is zero when (x′, y′) lies on the heading line (straight motion). Code needs a straight-line branch: v̂ = signed distance/Δt, ω̂ = 0.
Derive by hand. CODE: C3, Table 5.1 line 2. TEST: plug the solution back into both equalities of (5.17).
Implement. Δθ is the turned angle along the circle. PITFALL: the difference of two atan2's needs wrap(); without it a small turn across ±π reads as ±2π.
DEFINE: atan2 as in every numerical library (np.arctan2, std::atan2); do not implement it.
Derive. Δdist = r*·Δθ. PITFALL: r* ≥ 0, so Δdist takes the sign of Δθ: a forward right turn gets a negative distance. This is where Table 5.1 line 7's sign error comes from.
Implement, with the sign fixed: v̂ must be positive when the robot moved forward along its initial heading. CODE: C3. TEST: right turn and reverse.
Implement. γ̂ = (θ′ − θ)/Δt − ω̂, with θ′ − θ wrapped. CODE: C3, Table 5.1 line 9.
Implement. The product of three independent error densities = Table 5.1 line 10. In practice return the log, a sum of three terms.

items.anchor: lines 2 to 9 are equivalent to Equations
items.note: CODE: the map from Table 5.1 to the equations. Use it to cite lines in C3.

items.anchor: technically the resulting values lie always in
items.note: PRINT ERROR: Table 5.4 line 2 returns half the sum of 12 draws from rand(−b, b), which lies in [−6b, 6b], not [−2b, 2b]. Its variance is b² (12 · (2b)²/12 · 1/4), checked in this repo.

items.anchor: Alternatively, one might want to use the odometry measurements
items.note: Must read 5.4.1–5.4.2 (40 min), skim 5.4.3 (10 min). Odometry as rotate–translate–rotate, three noise terms, no degeneracy.

items.anchor: Practical experience suggests that odometry, while still erroneous
items.note: WHY: the book says odometry is usually more accurate than the commands, for most commercial robots (pp. 121, 132). ROBOT: untested on the tracked robot; T5's simulated slip leaves odometry ahead once spins are modelled. Test it by logging both against a motion-capture run.

items.anchor: Figure 5.7
items.note: FIGURE: any planar pose change = turn to face the target, drive straight, turn to the final heading. Three numbers for three DoF: sufficient, and no degeneracy (p. 135).
Must read, 25 min. Table 5.5: decompose the odometry change and the hypothesized change the same way, score the three differences.

items.anchor: it is therefore common to consider odometry data as if it were control signals
items.note: WHY: the alternative is putting velocity in the state and odometry in the measurement update. ROBOT: FORGE does the latter in spirit: wheel odometry becomes a between-factor with its own covariance.

items.anchor: knowing this transformation would solve the robot localization problem
items.note: WHY: only differences of odometry are used; the odometry frame drifts. ROBOT: the same reason a factor graph uses relative-pose factors, never absolute odometry poses.

Lines 8 and 10 need the angular differences wrapped (p. 135). Note the variances use the hatted δ̂ here and the measured δ in Table 5.6; that is the book's choice, keep it.
DEFINE: the control is a pair of odometry poses (x̄ₜ₋₁, x̄ₜ) in the odometry frame. SHAPES: 2 × 3.

items.note: FIGURE: (a) typical α's, (b) large translational error, (c) large rotational error. Compare with Fig 5.3: at small Δt they converge (p. 136).

items.note: PITFALL: the book's warning. Wrap δrot1 − δ̂rot1 and δrot2 − δ̂rot2 with wrap(). The text writes δrot2 − δ̄rot2 (bar) for δrot2 − δ̂rot2 (hat), a print slip. TEST: a pose pair whose rotations straddle ±π.

items.anchor: This last step assumes independence between
items.note: PITFALL: independent rot and trans errors is an assumption; skid-steer couples them (turning causes slip). α₄ is the only cross term.

items.note: FIGURE: heading error early in the path becomes lateral spread later; the cloud widens fastest after the turns. SESSION: the session reproduces it with your own α's.
Implement. CODE: C4 odometry_params line 1. Wrap the result.

Implement. δtrans ≥ 0: a robot reversing is described as 'turn 180°, drive, turn 180°'. PITFALL: for a reversing robot δrot1 and δrot2 are near ±π and their noise terms α₁δ²rot1 blow up; some implementations allow negative δtrans instead (from outside the book).
Implement. Wrap δrot2.
Implement. Noise subtracted from the measured rotation; variance α₁δ²rot1 + α₂δ²trans.
Implement. Variance α₃δ²trans + α₄(δ²rot1 + δ²rot2).
Implement. Same α₁, α₂ as (5.37).

items.anchor: is the error in odometry, assuming of course that xt is the true ﬁnal pose
items.note: WHY: the density scores the hypothesized pose by how far its decomposition is from the measured one. (5.44)–(5.46) are the three factors of Table 5.5 line 11.
Must read, 25 min. Condition either motion model on a map by multiplying with p(xₜ ∣ m); fine for small steps, wrong for large ones.
DEFINE: the map-based motion model. The map tells you where the robot cannot be.

items.anchor: which works well if the distance between xt−1 and xt is small
items.note: WHY: the approximation checks only the end pose. The book's own bound: less than half a robot diameter per step.
Implement. CODE: C5 motion_model_with_map. p(xₜ) uniform is absorbed in η.

items.anchor: p(xt | m) = 0 if and only if the robot would be placed in an occupied grid cell
items.note: DEFINE: p(xₜ ∣ m) is a free-space indicator on the configuration space (obstacles grown by the robot radius, p. 141). ROBOT: the tracked robot's footprint is not a circle; grow by the footprint at θ, or by the circumscribed radius.

items.anchor: This algorithms bootstraps previous motion models
items.note: Implement. CODE: C5. PRINT ERROR: the sampler has two lines numbered 3. PITFALL: 'do … until π > 0' never ends if every sample is in an obstacle (the robot's belief is already inside a wall); cap the retries and return the last sample with weight 0.

items.anchor: the sampling algorithm returns a weighted sample
items.note: WHY: the weight π = p(xₜ ∣ m) multiplies into the particle's importance weight (ch. 4, line 5). For an occupancy indicator π is 0 or a constant, so the loop is rejection sampling.

items.anchor: CONFIGURATION SPACE
items.note: DEFINE: pose space with obstacles grown by the robot's shape. For a circular robot, grow by the radius; θ does not matter.

items.anchor: Velocity motion model (a) without a map and (b) conditioned on a map
items.note: FIGURE: (a) the velocity density; (b) the same times p(xₜ ∣ m). The mass behind the wall, marked (∗), is the approximation's failure: the robot would have passed through the obstacle.

items.anchor: This error is the result of checking model consistency at the
items.note: PITFALL: the end-pose check lets particles tunnel through thin walls on large steps. ROBOT: between sparse keyframes a robot can move more than half its body length; check the swept arc instead.
Derive. Bayes rule with m as the 'measurement'.
Derive. The approximation is the first line: p(m ∣ xₜ, uₜ, xₜ₋₁) replaced by p(m ∣ xₜ).
WHY: the one assumption of 5.5: the map is informative only about the end pose, not the path. It fails exactly when the path crosses an obstacle.

items.anchor: Our description also does not consider robot dynamics
items.note: PITFALL: no dynamics. ROBOT: the drone's state needs velocity (book exercises 1–3); the book's own suggestion is to extend the state by a velocity vector.
